citations.quote: The approach is applied to the SidSat mission, a 4U CubeSat featuring a modular architecture with core avionics, a robotic arm payload, and an onboard AI/ML experimentation module.

Requirements were allocated to model components, then verified using parameterized simulations. MATLAB was employed for mass, power, and thermal margin calculations; STK for orbital behavior assessment; Excel for value propagation and I/O management; and Teamcenter with AWS for model control and data traceability.
The proposed approach is implemented and validated through a detailed case study on the design and development of SidSat, a small satellite platform modeled in SysML using Cameo Systems Modeler.

The research framework is further grounded in design science principles, where engineered artifacts, such as SysML models, prioritization matrices, integration scripts, and simulation outputs, are subject to iterative evaluation and refinement.

Relationships, including 《allocate》, 《derive》, 《refine》, 《satisfy》, and 《verify》, are systematically applied to preserve traceability and maintain alignment between design intent, stakeholder needs, and evolving constraints.

By uniting these three pillars into a single methodological construct, the framework delivers a scalable and reusable systems engineering approach suitable for high-assurance, digitally integrated aerospace projects.

Tool interoperability is managed through data exchange formats such as CSV and XMI, along with custom integration scripts tailored to project-specific needs. Simulation outputs are reviewed to refine model constraints and improve design alignment.

Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs) are used to establish the hierarchical decomposition of the satellite into its core subsystems: command and data handling (C&DH), communications, payload, attitude determination and control system (ADCS), power, structure, and thermal management.

Activity Diagrams illustrate functional flows associated with key mission activities, including orbital insertion, deployment, robotic arm movement, and thermal management. Each activity encompasses a group of tasks or decisions, represented using control and object flows.

Because the model is executable, such checks are performed automatically as configurations change. This reduces the need for disconnected simulation tools and improves turnaround during iterative design.

The approach utilizes SysML outputs in conjunction with prioritization metrics, enabling iterative or real-time updates that facilitate flexible and traceable decision-making throughout the CubeSat lifecycle.

Requirements were initially elicited from stakeholder objectives, environmental constraints, and mission scenarios, then structured using Requirements Decomposition strategies. Priority rankings were iteratively refined using scenario-based evaluation informed by simulations conducted in MATLAB and STK.
This approach was used to identify high-priority requirements from 110 candidates spanning Functional (FR), Performance (PR), Battery Testing (BTR), and Environmental (EvR) categories for a CubeSat.
Outcome of Method 1: From a total of 110, the list was narrowed down to 30 high-priority requirements, centered on mission success, battery reliability, and environmental resilience.

While AHP offers depth and traceable logic, the Weighted Scoring Model prioritizes speed and adaptability. This distinction makes it a strong fit for dynamic systems engineering efforts where flexibility and timely stakeholder alignment are essential.

A platform-agnostic integration scheme links Cameo Systems Modeler with external applications, including MATLAB for control validation, STK for orbital simulations, Excel for tracking design parameters, Teamcenter for managing configurations and revisions, and AWS for secure cloud access.
MATLAB simulations feed quantitative data into the prioritization framework, supporting uncertainty quantification, trade space analysis, and scenario-based validation.
External analysis environments, such as MATLAB and STK, provide runtime data that directly link to requirement satisfaction criteria within SysML constraint elements (AGI, 2022).

However, some integration challenges were encountered, particularly in managing data transformations and exchanging semantics between tools (Voirin, 2017). These challenges were addressed through scripts, structured templates, and predefined configurations suited for reuse (INCOSE, 2015).

The simulation assesses available orbital power for SidSat using a .mat file with parameters and solar input data (No Magic, 2023). A MATLAB script calculates total and average power over a 167-hour span. Cameo's Activity Diagram organizes the simulation flow and calls MATLAB code via MathScript (AGI, 2022).

A key output of the simulation is the time-series plot of average power generation over the 167-hour orbital cycle, offering valuable insight into the variability and performance of the solar subsystem. The system records a mean power output of approximately 4.29 W, confirming alignment with design expectations and enabling verification of related system requirements.

Following that approach, the SidSat case study used the framework to evaluate a validated set of 113 actionable requirements derived from the complete requirement matrix within the SysML model.

Representative high-priority requirements, such as thermal envelope compliance, power budgeting, vibration survivability, and alignment precision, served as anchor cases to evaluate each platform's capacity to support modeling, simulation, and verification.

The process leading to this selection was systematic and traceable. From an initial pool of 113 validated requirements, 30 were elevated through Method 1 (filtration and scoring), then assessed across three modeling platforms in Method 2, and ranked in Method 3 via a decision matrix.

This toolchain achieves a closed-loop digital engineering workflow:
Phase 1 - Manual Parameter Entry and Static Validation: Initial simulation activities were conducted using manually defined parameters in SysML parametric diagrams.
Phase 3 - Full Automation with One-Click Execution: The final phase achieved full automation using the Cameo Simulation Toolkit.

Simulation outputs, such as power availability, thermal values, and object visibility counts, were automatically exported to Excel. These values were labeled, timestamped, and linked to their corresponding requirement identifiers.

The script computed the average power over a 167-hour period, yielding 4.29 W, which was then exported and compared against the defined operational requirement of 1-42 Wh (MathWorks, 2023). Cameo's internal constraint validation mechanism verified the result and updated the requirement to 'validated' (green).
Both methods were applied to a CubeSat case study decomposed into five subsystems: Payload, Power, Communication, Onboard Data Handling, and Attitude Control (Bricogne et al., 2020).
To establish a balanced comparison between OOSEM and Arcadia, a CubeSat modeling task was executed using both approaches.

Cameo offered faster diagram construction and easier customization, supporting quick iterations during logical decomposition and requirement mapping (Alai, 2019). However, this speed came with a higher burden of ensuring consistency across SysML views, especially when reusing behavior or structural elements.
However, the evaluation did not extend to full lifecycle validation, simulation integration, or post-deployment feedback loops (Alai, 2019).

Although Arcadia/Capella was initially included in the tool strategy, implementation was constrained by resource limitations, procedural restrictions, and access to the toolchain. As a result, Arcadia was applied conceptually to inform architectural comparisons but not used for full lifecycle modeling.
Within the SidSat project, requirements traceability was implemented through a rigorous, end-to-end Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach using SysML artifacts in Cameo Systems Modeler.
All these relationships were implemented within the Cameo model environment and visually managed through allocation matrices, dependency diagrams, and validation views.
Parameter mapping tables ensured that units, value types, and variable names remained consistent across tools.

Although formal hardware or software testing was outside the scope of this research, the toolchain integration activities conducted here represent a powerful surrogate, demonstrating that digital consistency and traceable validation can be achieved through simulation-based reasoning, parametric logic, and cross-domain tool interoperability.

Scenario-based system behavior assessment thus provided a robust foundation for early validation and design iteration. It exposed timing misalignments, subsystem dependencies, and performance bottlenecks that would be difficult to detect in purely static models.
The current Excel-heavy process still requires technical knowledge and constant manual oversight (Siddique, 2024).

Incompatibility across these tools, such as varying units, parameter mismatches, and version conflicts, initially hindered interoperability. These issues were addressed using predefined templates, automated scripts, and interface plugins.

Overall, the application of MBSE and digital engineering practices in SidSat improved verification accuracy, traceability, and lifecycle adaptability. Integration across engineering tools strengthened system-level analysis and streamlined data synchronization.

Many challenges emerged early, particularly those involving inconsistent data structures and unit misalignment across platforms (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022). These were gradually mitigated through rule-based formatting conventions and common schema alignment (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

This closed-loop response reduced dependence on postprocessing and shortened the redesign cycle (Madni et al., 2018). Performance risks that typically appear late in development were caught earlier through simulation-driven alerts (Browning et al., 2022).

This allowed controlled upgrades and reusable modules across similar subsystems (Siemens, 2022). Integration testing confirmed functional continuity even as scripts and parameters evolved (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022).

This workflow enables the structured sharing of parameters, scenario testing, and outcome validation using model-driven activity triggers, resulting in semi-automated simulation execution and test result propagation without reliance on hardware iterations (MathWorks, 2023).

First, the modeling and validation activities were confined to simulation-based environments and virtual toolchains, without incorporating physical subsystem testing or hardware-in-the-loop experimentation (INCOSE, 2015).

Third, while tool interoperability was demonstrated effectively, it was partially restricted by license availability, proprietary data structures, and manual interface configuration, which limited the depth of automation and increased overhead during cross-platform testing (Object Management Group, 2017).
Due to funding limitations, several doctoral-level research roles were phased out and replaced by entry-level interns with limited modeling experience.

All models, parameters, data values, and interface visuals presented in this dissertation are used solely for academic and experimental purposes. They have been adapted to support the SidSat case study and do not represent real mission specifications or any official government or agency project.
